# 1. 

## a.

$$
\text{Provided that}: \qquad \bar{Y} (A = 0, B = 0) = 1, \qquad \bar{Y} (A = 1, B = 0) = 5,
$$

$$
\bar{Y} (A = 0, B = 1) = 4, \qquad \bar{Y} (A = 1, B = 1) = 7
$$

> we can hold the following to be true.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{Y} (A = 0, B = 0) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i~|~A = 0, B = 0)   \\
= \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 0 + \beta_2 \cdot 0 + \beta_3 \cdot 0 + \epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + 0 = 1\\
\therefore \beta_0 = 1
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{Y} (A = 1, B = 0) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i~|~A = 1, B = 0)   \\
= \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 1 + \beta_2 \cdot 0 + \beta_3 \cdot 0 + \epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 + 0 + 0 + \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) \\ 
= 1 + \beta_1 + 0 = 5\\
\therefore \beta_1 = 4
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{Y} (A = 0, B = 1) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i~|~A = 0, B = 1)   \\
= \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 0 + \beta_2 \cdot 1 + \beta_3 \cdot 0 + \epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + 0 + \beta_2 + 0 + \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) \\ 
= 1 + \beta_2 + 0 = 4\\
\therefore \beta_2 = 3
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{Y} (A = 1, B = 1) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i~|~A = 1, B = 1)   \\
= \mathbb{E}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot 1 + \beta_2 \cdot 1 + \beta_3 \cdot 1 + \epsilon_i) \\ 
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 + \mathbb{E}(\epsilon_i) \\ 
= 1 + 4 + 3 + \beta_3 = 7\\
\therefore \beta_3 = -1
\end{aligned}
$$

> **Final Answer**: $\boxed{\beta_0 = 1, \beta_1 = 4, \beta_2 = 3, \beta_3 = -1}$

## b. 

> In order to get estimates for the four regression coefficients, we need estimates for the four averages above. We have two variables, $A$ and $B$, which can take values $0$ or $1$ depending on whether or not the value observed was at a "high" or "low" level for each. $\beta_0$, the intercept or "baseline", necessitates that we have a treatment group where $A = 0, B=0$. Then, by comparing to our baseline, we can get our treatment effects for $A$ and $B$ by changing the level one at a time: one group is $A=1, B=0$, and the other $A = 0, B=1$. This lets us estimate $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$. We also have to estimate the interaction effect $\beta_3$, so we need treatment group $A = 1, B = 1$. This constructs our full factorial design, where we have $2^2$ treatment groups, one for each combination of treatment levels. Then, our observational units are randomly assigned to evenly split among the treatment groups.

> In summary:

| Group | Treatment | Number of units |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|
|Group 1| $A = 0, B = 0$ |$n=50$|
|Group 2| $A = 1, B = 0$ |$n=50$|
|Group 3| $A = 0, B = 1$ |$n=50$|
|Group 4| $A = 1, B = 1$ |$n=50$|

## c. 

> *A full factorial design would be better:*

> We need to compare $A = 0,~ B = 0, ~C = 0$ and $A = 0, ~B = 0, ~C = 1$ to see C's treatment effect; i.e. how it changes the predicted result when all other variables are held constant. Then, to see how the effect changes for A and B, we need to compare $A = 0, ~B = 0,~ C = 1$ versus $A = 1,~ B = 0,~ C = 1$; likewise for B, we need to compare $ A = 0, ~B = 0, ~C = 1$ to $A = 0,~ B = 1,~ C = 1$. Assuming that our treatment groups from **(b)** had level $C = 0$, then this introduces 3 new groups. That gives us 7 treatment groups to estimate the interaction effects described.

> A full factorial design would also include a three-way interaction effect, getting us $7 + 1 = 2^3$ groups, each group getting 25 units through random assignment. While a three-way interaction effect was not mentioned in the prompt, we also don't have reasonable certainty to assume that interaction effect to be zero. So, if we did a partial factorial design, we would be makiing the dubious assumption that there is no three-way interaction effect, and we would also be missing the interactions between $C$ and $A$ or $B$, or we would be missing treatment effects.
